newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece to unveil tight 1997 budget in drive to EMU.
newsitem.headline: Greece to unveil tight 1997 budget in drive to EMU.

text.p: Greece's socialist government is due to unveil details of a tight 1997 budget on Tuesday that should pave the way for joining Europe's monetary union either at the turn of the century or within the following two years.

The cabinet is going to convene on Tuesday morning to discuss the budget, seen to entail increased taxation, and Prime Minister Costas Simitis is expected to present its outline to reporters afterwards.
The final and official presentation of the 1997 budget will take place in late November, government officials told Reuters.

Simitis, who won a fresh four-year popular mandate in elections in September, is expected to make sure Greece's commitment to Economic Monetary Union (EMU) is visible in the budget. The budget is set to stick to an earlier convergence plan aiming at align the economy with the rest of the European Union.
"The cost of non-participation in the European Monetary Union in huge," Simitis told the socialist party's central committee and parliamentary group on Monday.
The government is expected to announce that the 1997 general government budget deficit will fall to 4.2 percent of GDP in line with the convergence plan, from an expected 7.6 percent this year.
The budget deficit is scheduled to drop to 2.4 percent of GDP in 1998, well below the three percent target needed to join the monetary union.
According to press leaks, the fiscal consolidation in 1997 will be based on boosting tax and non-tax revenues and applying a freeze in real spending.

The budget deficit reduction in 1997 will come from savings of one trillion drachmas or more which will be the result of a high revenue growth rate of about 15 percent or more and an increase in nominal expenditures between six and seven percent.

Revenues will grow from increased direct taxes, as many tax breaks will be abolished as well as the non-indexation of the income tax scale for the fifth straight year. A host of new taxes on real estate, interest on state securities and financial products will be introduced.

A withholding tax of 7.5 percent is to be applied to interest earned on new government securities effective early December or January 1997 and a 15 percent tax will be levied on financial products including derivatives.

Mutual funds will face a new tax of between 0.2 and 0.5 percent on their assets under management but it is still unclear whether the current 15 percent withholding tax on income from state securities and repos will be maintained.
Commercial banks are also likely to see their corporate marginal tax rate go up to 40 percent from 35 percent.

A pick-up in indirect taxes will also correspond to stronger GDP growth, forecasted at 3.3 percent in 1997, upr from expected 2.6 percent in 1996. It will be accompanied by another attempt to crack down on tax evasion.

Spending is likely to be projected to rise about six percent, about the same as projected average inflation. The wage bill will likely rise by about 8.5 percent and interest payments on public debt by much less.
But capital expenditures are expected to soar to about 30 percent to make sure that Greece absorbs all of its European Union funds to fuel economic growth.
The government has already submitted a draft bill to parliament comprised of 14 measures to control spending and do away with some public sector waste.

New hirings with the exception of teachers will be limited to 20 percent of retirements, subsidies to public utilities will be curtailed and many off-budget items that have been partly blamed for a high debt to GDP ratio will be included in the budget.
Greece's debt to GDP ratio, at around 100 percent, has failed to record a noticeable improvement despite falling interest rates on public debt and larger primary surpluses as a percent of GDP.
"Below the line" items such as the issuance of restructuring bonds for state banks and public organisations are mainly responsible for a stubborn debt-to-GDP ratio. -- Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
